key_terms.term: Symbol period T, symbol rate R<sub>s</sub>
key_terms.meaning: One symbol every T seconds; R<sub>s</sub> = 1/T baud and R<sub>b</sub> = R<sub>s</sub> log₂M bit/s.
y(kT) = a<sub>k</sub>p(0) + Σ<sub>n≠k</sub> a<sub>n</sub>p((k − n)T) + noise; worst case D = Σ<sub>n≠0</sub>|p(nT)|/p(0).
p(nT) = 0 for every n ≠ 0; in frequency Σ<sub>m</sub> P(f − m/T) = T·p(0).
B<sub>N</sub> = R<sub>s</sub>/2 = 1/(2T), the least bandwidth for zero ISI.
B = (R<sub>s</sub>/2)(1 + α), excess αR<sub>s</sub>/2, roll-off 0 ≤ α ≤ 1.
√P(f) at the transmitter and at the receiver: zero ISI and a matched receive filter together.
Overlaid symbol-clock-triggered traces; vertical opening = noise margin, horizontal opening = timing margin.
2N + 1 taps solving Σ c<sub>k</sub>h<sub>m−k</sub> = δ<sub>m</sub> for |m| ≤ N; noise power × Σc<sub>k</sub>².
c<sub>k</sub>(n + 1) = c<sub>k</sub>(n) + μ e(n) x(n − k), with e(n) = d(n) − y(n).
⟨x, y⟩ = ∫₀ᵀ x(t)y(t) dt; E = ⟨s, s⟩ = Σ s<sub>i</sub>²; d² = Σ(s<sub>mi</sub> − s<sub>ni</sub>)².
φ<sub>1</sub> = s<sub>1</sub>/‖s<sub>1</sub>‖; g<sub>m</sub> = s<sub>m</sub> − Σ⟨s<sub>m</sub>, φ<sub>i</sub>⟩φ<sub>i</sub>; new axis g<sub>m</sub>/‖g<sub>m</sub>‖ if nonzero; N ≤ M.
h(t) = s(T − t); output E at t = T; maximum SNR 2E/N₀.
z(T) = ∫₀ᵀ r(t)s(t) dt, the same sample as the matched filter at t = T.
Choose the nearest s<sub>m</sub>, or the largest ⟨r, s<sub>m</sub>⟩ − E<sub>m</sub>/2.
P<sub>e</sub> = Q(d/√(2N₀)); polar binary Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N₀)); on-off Q(√(E<sub>b</sub>/N₀)).
c<sub>k</sub> = a<sub>k</sub> + a<sub>k−1</sub> (1 + D) with precoder p<sub>k</sub> = b<sub>k</sub> ⊕ p<sub>k−1</sub>; P<sub>e</sub> = 1.5 Q((π/4)√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N₀)).

takeaways: ISI is the sum of the neighbours' pulse samples at the sampling instant; peak distortion measures its worst case.
Nyquist's criterion p(nT) = 0 for n ≠ 0 gives zero ISI and sets the least bandwidth at R<sub>s</sub>/2.
The raised cosine spends αR<sub>s</sub>/2 extra hertz for a buildable filter and tails that fall as 1/t³; split as two root raised cosines it also gives a matched receiver.
The eye pattern shows the noise margin (vertical opening) and the timing margin (horizontal opening) at a glance.
A zero-forcing equalizer solves linear equations for its taps and removes ISI near the centre at the cost of noise gain Σc<sub>k</sub>²; LMS learns the taps and tends to the MMSE setting.
Gram-Schmidt turns M waveforms into points in N ≤ M dimensions, where energy is squared length and distance decides errors.
The matched filter and the correlator give the same sample, with the largest possible SNR 2E/N₀, at t = T only.
In AWGN the ML detector picks the nearest point; P<sub>e</sub> = Q(d/√(2N₀)) per pair, Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N₀)) for polar binary.
Precoded duobinary sends binary data in R<sub>s</sub>/2 with a buildable filter at a 2.1 dB cost; M-PAM divides the bandwidth by log₂M at about 4 dB per extra bit for small M.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the zero-ISI condition with the raised cosine bandwidth, the matched filter proof with its 2E/N₀ result, and the error probability of binary signalling; equalizers, Gram-Schmidt and duobinary come as one long question each. Every model answer below works its numbers in full.

bank.q: Define intersymbol interference. Derive the condition for zero ISI at the sampling instants, state Nyquist's criterion in the time and frequency domains, and find the least bandwidth it allows.
outline: Received signal r(t) = Σ a<sub>n</sub>p(t − nT) + n(t) and its sample y(kT)
The ISI term and peak distortion
Zero ISI: p(nT) = 0 for n ≠ 0
Frequency form Σ<sub>m</sub> P(f − m/T) = T·p(0)
Least bandwidth R<sub>s</sub>/2 with the sinc pulse, and why the sinc is impractical
answer: Model. A baseband link sends symbols an every T seconds. The transmit filter, channel and receive filter together give one overall pulse p(t), so the waveform at the sampler is r(t) = Σn anp(t − nT) + n(t), where n(t) is noise.

answer.text: Sample. Sampling at t = kT to decide symbol k and separating the term n = k:
answer.pre:
y(kT) = a<sub>k</sub>·p(0)  +  Σ<sub>n≠k</sub> a<sub>n</sub>·p((k − n)T)  +  n(kT)
          wanted            intersymbol interference      noise

answer: Definition. Intersymbol interference (ISI) is the middle sum: the contribution of the tails of other symbols' pulses at the instant symbol k is sampled. In the worst data pattern every term pushes the same way, so the worst-case ISI as a fraction of the wanted sample is the peak distortion D = Σn≠0|p(nT)|/p(0). If D ≥ 1, some patterns are decided wrongly even without noise.

Condition for zero ISI. The middle sum is zero for every data pattern only if each coefficient is zero: p(nT) = 0 for every integer n ≠ 0, with p(0) ≠ 0. This is Nyquist's first criterion in the time domain. It says nothing about p(t) between the sampling instants.

answer.text: Frequency domain. The samples p(nT) form the sequence p(0)δ[n]. Sampling p(t) every T seconds makes its spectrum periodic: the spectrum of the samples is (1/T)ΣmP(f − m/T). A sequence that is p(0) at n = 0 and zero elsewhere has a flat spectrum p(0). Equating the two:
answer.pre: Σ<sub>m</sub> P(f − m/T) = T·p(0)    for all f

answer: So the copies of P(f), shifted by every multiple of 1/T, must add up to a constant.

Least bandwidth. If P(f) were zero above some W < 1/(2T), copies spaced 1/T apart would leave gaps between W and 1/T − W where the sum is zero, not constant. So W ≥ 1/(2T). The only spectrum that reaches W = 1/(2T) is the rectangle P(f) = T·p(0) for |f| < 1/(2T), whose pulse is p(t) = p(0)·sin(πt/T)/(πt/T), the sinc. The Nyquist bandwidth is therefore BN = 1/(2T) = Rs/2.

Numbers. A binary link at 2400 bit/s has Rs = 2400 baud and needs at least 1200 Hz. With p(0) = 1, p(±T) = 0.25 and neighbours +1, +1 around a −1 symbol, the ISI is +0.5 and the sample is −0.5: the decision is still right, but half the noise margin is gone (D = 0.5).

Why not the sinc. It is non-causal (it extends to −∞), and its tails fall only as 1/t. With a sampling error of 0.1T the six nearest neighbours alone give D = 0.369, and the sum keeps growing with more neighbours. Practical systems therefore use a raised cosine, which meets the same criterion with bandwidth (Rs/2)(1 + α).
Check. For the sinc, p(nT) = sin(nπ)/(nπ) = 0 for n ≠ 0, and its rectangle of height T and width 1/T, copied every 1/T, tiles the frequency axis to the constant T, as the criterion requires.

bank.q: Explain the raised cosine spectrum and pulse, the role of the roll-off factor, and why a link uses a root raised cosine filter at each end. Explain how an eye pattern is produced and what it shows. Illustrate with a 4800 baud binary link and α = 0.5.
outline: Brick-wall problem; odd-symmetric roll-off still meets Nyquist
Spectrum regions and B = (R<sub>s</sub>/2)(1 + α); pulse formula and 1/t³ tails
RRC split: zero ISI plus matched filter
Eye pattern: how it is made; vertical and horizontal opening, slope, crossings
Numbers for 4800 baud, α = 0.5
answer: The problem. Zero ISI in the least bandwidth Rs/2 needs a rectangular spectrum (the sinc pulse), which cannot be built and whose 1/t tails make the ISI large under any timing error.

The idea. Nyquist's criterion only asks that the copies P(f − m/T) add to a constant. If the spectrum falls around Rs/2 with odd symmetry, what one copy loses below Rs/2 the next copy adds above it. The raised cosine uses half a cosine period for this fall.

answer.text: Spectrum. With f1 = (1 − α)Rs/2 and B = (1 + α)Rs/2:
answer.pre:
P(f) = T                                       for |f| ≤ f<sub>1</sub>
P(f) = (T/2)[1 + cos(π(|f| − f<sub>1</sub>)/(αR<sub>s</sub>))]   for f<sub>1</sub> ≤ |f| ≤ B
P(f) = 0                                       for |f| ≥ B

answer: Roll-off factor. α (0 ≤ α ≤ 1) is the excess bandwidth as a fraction of Rs/2: excess = αRs/2. α = 0 is the sinc; α = 1 doubles the band to Rs.
The sinc factor keeps the zeros at t = nT (zero ISI); the second factor makes the tails fall as 1/t³. At t = 2.5T the sinc is still 0.127, while the α = 0.5 pulse is 0.017.

Root raised cosine pair. The receive filter should also be matched to the arriving pulse, to give the best SNR at the sampling instant. Put |GT(f)| = |GR(f)| = √P(f): the receive filter is then matched to the transmit pulse, and the cascade GTGR = P(f) is the raised cosine, so the overall pulse has zero ISI. One RRC alone is not a Nyquist pulse; only the pair is.

Eye pattern: how it is made. The receive-filter output goes to an oscilloscope whose sweep is triggered by the recovered symbol clock and lasts about two symbol periods. Random data makes thousands of different traces, which overlap on the screen; for binary data they leave an open region shaped like an eye.

head: Feature
Meaning
rows: Vertical opening at the sampling instant
Range of sampling times that still decide correctly: the timing margin
Slope of the traces near the centre
How fast the margin shrinks with timing error
Timing jitter seen by the clock recovery
Where the vertical opening is largest

answer: Check. 3600 − 2400 = 1200 Hz = αRs/2, and the eye at the exact centre has opening 2 (every trace passes ±1), because the raised cosine is zero at every other sampling instant.

bank.q: Describe the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization procedure. Show that the residual at each step is orthogonal to the earlier axes and that M signals need at most M dimensions. Illustrate with s<sub>1</sub>(t) = 1 V on 0 to 1 ms, s<sub>2</sub>(t) = 2 V on the first half and 0 on the second, and s<sub>3</sub>(t) = 0 on the first half and 2 V on the second.
outline: Inner product, energy, orthonormal basis
Steps: normalise, project, subtract, normalise or skip
Proof of orthogonality of the residual
N ≤ M and when N < M
Worked illustration: axes, coordinates, energies, distances
answer: Definitions. For real signals on 0 ≤ t ≤ T the inner product is ⟨x, y⟩ = ∫₀ᵀ x(t)y(t) dt, the energy is E = ⟨s, s⟩ and the norm is ‖s‖ = √E. A set φ1 … φN is orthonormal if ⟨φi, φj⟩ = 1 for i = j and 0 otherwise.

answer.pre:
1. φ<sub>1</sub> = s<sub>1</sub>/‖s<sub>1</sub>‖
2. for m = 2 … M:
     c<sub>i</sub> = ⟨s<sub>m</sub>, φ<sub>i</sub>⟩ for every axis found so far
     g<sub>m</sub>(t) = s<sub>m</sub>(t) − Σ c<sub>i</sub>φ<sub>i</sub>(t)
     if ‖g<sub>m</sub>‖ > 0: new axis φ = g<sub>m</sub>/‖g<sub>m</sub>‖
     else: no new axis (s<sub>m</sub> is a combination of the old ones)

answer: Orthogonality. For any old axis φk: ⟨gm, φk⟩ = ⟨sm, φk⟩ − Σi ci⟨φi, φk⟩. Orthonormality leaves only i = k, so this is ck − ck = 0. Dividing by ‖gm‖ gives unit energy, so the enlarged set is still orthonormal.
Dimension. Each signal adds at most one axis, so N ≤ M. Equality holds only if the signals are linearly independent; any signal that is a combination of earlier ones has gm = 0 and adds nothing.
Coordinates. Every signal is then sm(t) = Σ smiφi(t) with smi = ⟨sm, φi⟩. Energies and distances become vector lengths: Em = Σ smi², dmn² = Σ(smi − sni)².

head: Step
Working
Result
rows: 0 on both halves: no new axis

answer: So N = 2 for M = 3, because s<sub>3</sub> = 2s<sub>1</sub> − s<sub>2</sub>. The points are s<sub>1</sub> = (1, 0), s<sub>2</sub> = (1, 1), s<sub>3</sub> = (1, −1) V·√ms.
Energies and distances. E1 = 1, E2 = E3 = 2 V²·ms; d12 = d13 = 1 and d23 = 2 V·√ms.
Order. Starting with s2 instead gives φ1 = s2/√2 and s2 = (√2, 0): the coordinates change, but energies and distances do not.
Check. From the waveforms, E2 = 2² × 0.5 = 2 and d23² = ∫(s2 − s3)² = 4 × 0.5 + 4 × 0.5 = 4, so d23 = 2: both agree with the vector results.

bank.q: Define the matched filter. Prove that it maximises the output SNR at the sampling instant in white noise, find that maximum, and show that the correlation receiver gives the same sample. Evaluate for a 1 V, 1 ms rectangular pulse with N₀ = 2 × 10⁻⁶ W/Hz.
outline: Model: r(t) = s(t) + w(t), PSD N₀/2
Output signal and noise variance at t = T
Cauchy-Schwarz bound and equality: h(t) = s(T − t)
Maximum SNR 2E/N₀; frequency response
Correlator equivalence; numbers
answer: Model. A known pulse s(t), 0 ≤ t ≤ T, with energy E = ∫s²dt, arrives with white Gaussian noise w(t) of two-sided PSD N₀/2. A linear filter h(t) is followed by a sampler at t = T.

answer.pre:
signal:   y<sub>s</sub>(T) = ∫ h(τ) s(T − τ) dτ
noise:    σ² = (N₀/2) ∫ h²(τ) dτ
SNR = y<sub>s</sub>²(T) / σ²

answer.text: Bound. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, (∫ab)² ≤ ∫a² · ∫b², with a = h(τ) and b = s(T − τ):
answer.pre:
[∫ h(τ)s(T − τ)dτ]² ≤ ∫h²(τ)dτ · ∫s²(T − τ)dτ = ∫h²dτ · E

SNR ≤ (∫h²dτ · E) / ((N₀/2)∫h²dτ) = 2E/N₀

answer: Equality. Cauchy-Schwarz is an equality only when a ∝ b, that is h(τ) = k·s(T − τ). The gain k cancels in the SNR, so take k = 1: the matched filter is h(t) = s(T − t), the pulse reversed in time and delayed by T. Its transfer function is H(f) = S*(f)e−j2πfT: it passes each frequency in proportion to how much of the pulse is there, and lines up all phases at t = T.
Maximum. With h = s(T − t): ys(T) = ∫s²dτ = E and σ² = (N₀/2)E, so SNRmax = E²/((N₀/2)E) = 2E/N₀. It depends only on the energy, not the shape.

answer.text: Correlator. The correlation receiver forms z(T) = ∫₀ᵀ r(t)s(t)dt. In the matched filter put h(τ) = s(T − τ) and u = T − τ:
answer.pre: y(T) = ∫ s(T − τ) r(T − τ) dτ = ∫₀ᵀ s(u) r(u) du = z(T)

answer: The two give the same sample at T, hence the same decisions. Between samples they differ: the matched-filter output for a rectangle is a triangle, the correlator output a ramp that is dumped at T.

Output waveform. For the 1 V, 1 ms rectangle the matched filter is the same rectangle, and its signal output is a triangle: 0.5 × 10⁻³ at t = 0.5 ms, the peak 1 × 10⁻³ at t = T = 1 ms, 0.5 × 10⁻³ at 1.5 ms and zero at 2 ms. The noise variance is 1 × 10⁻⁹ at every instant, so the SNR is largest only at the peak; at 0.8 ms it is 0.8² × 1000 = 640.

Interpretation. In frequency, |H(f)| = |S(f)|: the filter lets through the frequencies where the pulse has energy and rejects noise elsewhere, and the factor e−j2πfT lines up all their phases at t = T. That is why every part of the pulse adds in phase at the sampling instant and nowhere else.
Check. 2E/N₀ = 2 × 10⁻³/(2 × 10⁻⁶) = 1000, the same as E²/σ². Writing E/N₀ = 500 (27 dB) would be the common 3 dB slip.

bank.q: Explain duobinary signalling. Why does a deliberately introduced ISI let binary data use only R<sub>s</sub>/2 of bandwidth with a realisable filter? Explain error propagation and how precoding removes it, tracing the bits 1 0 1 1 with p<sub>0</sub> = 0.
outline: Coder c<sub>k</sub> = a<sub>k</sub> + a<sub>k−1</sub> (1 + D), three levels
Overall response 2T cos(πfT) in |f| ≤ R<sub>s</sub>/2, smooth band edge
Decoding by subtraction and error propagation
Precoder p<sub>k</sub> = b<sub>k</sub> ⊕ p<sub>k−1</sub> and the |c<sub>k</sub>| rule
Trace and the 2.1 dB cost
answer: Coder. Polar symbols ak = ±1 pass through ck = ak + ak−1, so each sample holds the current symbol plus a known copy of the previous one. The levels are −2, 0 and +2. In delay-operator form the coder is 1 + D.

answer.text: Spectrum. The coder's response is 1 + e−j2πfT; followed by an ideal Nyquist filter of bandwidth 1/(2T):

answer: |H(f)| falls smoothly to zero at the band edge f = 1/(2T) instead of dropping like a brick wall, so a real filter can approximate it. The bandwidth stays R<sub>s</sub>/2, so binary data still reaches 2 bit/s/Hz. The known ISI is what shaped the spectrum.
Error propagation. Without precoding the receiver recovers âk = ck − âk−1. If one decision is wrong, the next subtraction uses the wrong âk−1, and the error carries forward to every later symbol.

Precoder. Before the coder form pk = bk ⊕ pk−1 (starting from p0 = 0) and send ak = 2pk − 1. Then ck = 0 when pk ≠ pk−1, that is when bk = 1, and ck = ±2 when bk = 0. The receiver rule is: |ck| < 1 → 1, |ck| > 1 → 0. It uses only the current sample, so one level error costs one bit.
The decoded bits 1 0 1 1 equal the input. If c<sub>2</sub> were misread as 0, only b̂<sub>2</sub> would be wrong.

Cost. The middle level has two thresholds and the 1 + D shaping costs transmit energy; with the filter split equally and symbol-by-symbol decisions, Pe = 1.5 Q((π/4)√(2Eb/N₀)), a loss of 20 log₁₀(4/π) = 2.1 dB against ideal binary.
Check. At Eb/N₀ = 10 dB: (π/4)√20 = 3.512, Q(3.512) = 2.22 × 10⁻⁴, Pe = 3.33 × 10⁻⁴, against 3.87 × 10⁻⁶ for ideal binary.

bank.q: A binary baseband system sends 2400 symbols per second through a raised cosine system with α = 0.5. Find the symbol period, the Nyquist bandwidth, the transmission bandwidth and the excess bandwidth. Repeat for α = 0, 0.25 and 1, and comment on the eye opening when the sampler is 0.1T late.
outline: T = 1/R<sub>s</sub>
Nyquist bandwidth R<sub>s</sub>/2 = 1200 Hz
B = (R<sub>s</sub>/2)(1 + α); excess αR<sub>s</sub>/2
Table for α = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1
Trade-off: bandwidth against filter difficulty and timing tolerance
answer: Symbol period. T = 1/Rs = 1/2400 s = 416.7 µs.
Nyquist bandwidth. BN = Rs/2 = 1200 Hz. Binary means Rb = Rs = 2400 bit/s.

answer.text: All four roll-offs. The last column is the worst-case sample of a +1 symbol, over every pattern of neighbours, when sampled 0.1T late (from the pulse formula).

answer: Comment on α = 0. It uses the least bandwidth but needs a brick-wall filter, which cannot be built, and its 1/t tails make the timing-error ISI grow without limit as more neighbours are counted.

Comment on larger α. More bandwidth buys a gentler filter and tails that fall as 1/t³, so the eye stays open over a wider range of sampling instants: at 0.1T late the worst sample is 0.652 for α = 0.25 but 0.896 for α = 1. α = 1 also puts extra zeros halfway between the later instants (±1.5T, ±2.5T, …), which helps clock recovery.

Spectrum shapes. For α = 0.5 the spectrum is flat up to 600 Hz and falls as half a cosine to zero at 1800 Hz, passing through half height at 1200 Hz. For α = 0.25 the flat part runs to 900 Hz and the fall ends at 1500 Hz; for α = 1 there is no flat part and the fall spans 0 to 2400 Hz.
Reverse use. If the channel offered only 1500 Hz, the largest roll-off would be α = 2 × 1500/2400 − 1 = 0.25; at 1800 Hz it would be 0.5. The formula B = (Rs/2)(1 + α) works in both directions.
Choice. α = 0.25 to 0.5 is the usual compromise: 25 % to 50 % more bandwidth than the minimum for a buildable filter and a comfortable timing margin.
Check. Each excess equals αRs/2: 0.25 × 1200 = 300, 0.5 × 1200 = 600, 1 × 1200 = 1200 Hz, as in the table.

bank.q: A channel has the sampled response h(−T) = 0.1, h(0) = 0.8, h(T) = 0.3, all other samples zero. Design a three-tap zero-forcing equalizer, find the equalized response from −2T to 2T, the peak distortion before and after, and the effect on the SNR of white noise.
outline: Convolution v<sub>m</sub> = Σ c<sub>k</sub>h<sub>m−k</sub>
Three equations: v<sub>−1</sub> = 0, v<sub>0</sub> = 1, v<sub>1</sub> = 0
Solve for c<sub>−1</sub>, c<sub>0</sub>, c<sub>1</sub>
Residual ISI at ±2T; peak distortion
Noise enhancement Σc<sub>k</sub>²
answer: Set-up. h−1 = 0.1, h0 = 0.8, h1 = 0.3. With taps c−1, c0, c1 the equalized response is vm = c−1hm+1 + c0hm + c1hm−1.
Solve. From the first, c−1 = −0.125c0; from the third, c1 = −0.375c0. Substituting in the second: c0(−0.0375 + 0.8 − 0.0375) = 0.725c0 = 1, so c0 = 1.3793. Then c−1 = −0.1724 and c1 = −0.5172.

Peak distortion. Before: (0.1 + 0.3)/0.8 = 0.5. After: (0.0172 + 0.1552)/1 = 0.172. The equalizer removes the ISI at ±T but creates smaller ISI at ±2T, because three taps can force only three conditions.
Noise. White noise samples of variance σ² leave the equalizer with variance σ²Σck² = σ²(0.0297 + 1.9025 + 0.2675) = 2.200σ².

SNR effect. Before the equalizer the wanted sample is 0.8 with noise σ², SNR ∝ 0.64/σ². After it the sample is 1 with noise 2.200σ², SNR ∝ 0.4545/σ². The ratio 0.4545/0.64 = 0.710 is a 1.49 dB loss of SNR, the price of removing the ISI: noise enhancement.

Frequency view. The channel's response H(f) = 0.1ej2πfT + 0.8 + 0.3e−j2πfT has |H| from 1.2 at f = 0 down to 0.4 at f = 1/(2T), a 3 to 1 tilt. The equalizer's |C| rises from 0.690 at f = 0 to 2.069 at 1/(2T): it boosts exactly where the channel is weak, which is where the noise is boosted too. The product |C·H| now stays between 0.828 and 1.172 instead of being flat, because three taps cannot invert H(f) exactly.
Comment. A five-tap equalizer would also force v±2 = 0 but would raise the noise gain further. Where the noise matters more than the ISI, an MMSE equalizer balances the two.
Check. v0 = −0.0517 + 1.1034 − 0.0517 = 1.0000 and v±1 = 0 to four decimals, so the taps satisfy all three equations.

bank.q: A polar (antipodal) binary baseband system uses pulses of energy E<sub>b</sub> in AWGN of two-sided density N₀/2. Find the bit error probability at E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ = 10 dB and at 7 dB, and compare with on-off signalling at the same average E<sub>b</sub>/N₀. Use Q(4.472) = 3.87 × 10⁻⁶, Q(3.166) = 7.73 × 10⁻⁴, Q(3.162) = 7.83 × 10⁻⁴ and Q(2.239) = 1.26 × 10⁻².
outline: Points ±√E<sub>b</sub>, distance 2√E<sub>b</sub>
P<sub>e</sub> = Q(d/√(2N₀)) = Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N₀))
Convert dB to ratio, then evaluate
On-off: d = √(2E<sub>b</sub>), P<sub>e</sub> = Q(√(E<sub>b</sub>/N₀))
Comment on the steep fall of Q
answer: Signal space. Polar signalling uses s1 = +√Ebφ1 and s2 = −√Ebφ1, so d = 2√Eb. The noise along φ1 has variance N₀/2.

answer.text: Error probability. An error needs the noise to cross the midpoint, a distance d/2 = √Eb:

answer: Where Q comes from. If +√Eb is sent, the correlator output is z = √Eb + w with w Gaussian, mean 0, variance N₀/2. The threshold is 0, so P(error | +) = P(w < −√Eb) = Q(√Eb/σ) with σ = √(N₀/2). By symmetry P(error | −) is the same, so with equal priors the average is the same Q value.
On-off. Points 0 and √(2Eb) have average energy Eb and distance d = √(2Eb), so Pe = Q(√(2Eb)/√(2N₀)) = Q(√(Eb/N₀)).

Comments. A 3 dB drop from 10 to 7 dB raises the polar error rate by a factor of about 200. On-off at 10 dB is almost exactly as good as polar at 7 dB (7.83 × 10⁻⁴ against 7.73 × 10⁻⁴), which is the 3 dB advantage of antipodal signals: their distance is √2 times larger for the same average energy.
Common slips. Putting 10 instead of 101.0 into the exponent of a dB value, or dropping the 2 in √(2Eb/N₀), which silently costs 3 dB.

Design view. For a target of 10⁻⁵, polar needs Q(x) = 10⁻⁵, x = 4.265, Eb/N₀ = x²/2 = 9.09 (9.59 dB); on-off needs x² = 18.2 (12.6 dB). At 10 dB polar has about 0.4 dB to spare; on-off falls short by 2.6 dB.
Check. Q(4.472) must lie between Q(4.5) = 3.40 × 10⁻⁶ and Q(4) = 3.17 × 10⁻⁵, and it does.

bank.q: Four equally likely signals on 0 ≤ t ≤ 3 ms are: s<sub>1</sub> = 1 V on 0 to 1 ms; s<sub>2</sub> = 1 V on 0 to 2 ms; s<sub>3</sub> = 1 V on 1 to 3 ms; s<sub>4</sub> = 1 V on 0 to 3 ms (zero elsewhere). Use Gram-Schmidt to find the basis and the signal points, give the dimension, find d<sub>min</sub>, and estimate the symbol error probability in AWGN with N₀ = 0.05 V²·ms.
outline: Energies and inner products
φ<sub>1</sub>, φ<sub>2</sub>, φ<sub>3</sub> by Gram-Schmidt; s<sub>4</sub> dependent
Coordinates and distance table
d<sub>min</sub> and nearest neighbours
P<sub>e</sub> ≈ N̄<sub>min</sub>Q(d<sub>min</sub>/√(2N₀)) and the full union bound
answer: Slots. Every signal is constant on the three 1 ms slots, so write it as its three levels: s1 = [1, 0, 0], s2 = [1, 1, 0], s3 = [0, 1, 1], s4 = [1, 1, 1] V. An inner product is Σ(level products) × 1 ms.
φ1. E1 = 1 V²·ms, so φ1 = s1/1 = 1/√ms on slot 1.
φ2. ⟨s2, φ1⟩ = 1; g2 = s2 − φ1 = 1 V on slot 2; ‖g2‖ = 1, so φ2 = 1/√ms on slot 2.
φ3. ⟨s3, φ1⟩ = 0, ⟨s3, φ2⟩ = 1; g3 = s3 − φ2 = 1 V on slot 3; φ3 = 1/√ms on slot 3.
s4. Projections 1, 1, 1; g4 = s4 − φ1 − φ2 − φ3 = 0. No new axis: N = 3 for M = 4.
dmin. dmin = 1 V·√ms. Neighbours at that distance: s1 has 1 (s2), s2 has 2 (s1, s4), s3 has 1 (s4), s4 has 2 (s2, s3); average N̄min = 6/4 = 1.5.
Nearest-neighbour estimate. Pe ≈ 1.5 × 7.83 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.17 × 10⁻³.
Average: (7.87 + 15.7 + 7.87 + 15.7) × 10⁻⁴/4 = 1.18 × 10⁻³, almost the same as the nearest-neighbour estimate, because the farther pairs add very little.

Receiver. Because the axes are the three 1 ms slots, the correlation receiver is three integrate-and-dump circuits, one per slot (each scaled by 1/√ms). A received r = (0.9, 0.8, 0.2) is at distances 0.831, 0.300, 1.221 and 0.831 from s1 … s4, so it is decided as s2. The metric ⟨r, sm⟩ − Em/2 gives 0.4, 0.7, 0.0 and 0.4 and agrees; the energies differ (1, 2, 2, 3), so the −Em/2 term must be kept.
Check. Energies from the waveforms: s4 is 1 V for 3 ms, so E4 = 3, matching 1² + 1² + 1².

bank.q: A 16-level PAM system sends 64 kbit/s over a baseband channel with raised cosine pulses of α = 0.25. Find the symbol rate, the bandwidth, and the bandwidth binary signalling would need. Derive the symbol error probability of M-PAM and evaluate it, with the Gray-coded bit error rate, at E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ = 22 dB. How much more E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ than binary does 16-PAM need for P<sub>e</sub> = 10⁻⁵?
outline: log₂16 = 4; R<sub>s</sub> = 16 000 baud; B = 10 kHz; binary 40 kHz
Levels ±d … ±15d; E<sub>s</sub> = (M² − 1)d²/3
Inner and end levels; P<sub>e</sub> = 2(1 − 1/M)Q(√(6E<sub>s</sub>/((M² − 1)N₀)))
Numbers at 22 dB; BER ≈ P<sub>e</sub>/4
Required E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ 23.14 dB against 9.59 dB
answer: Rates. 16 levels carry log₂16 = 4 bits, so Rs = 64 000/4 = 16 000 baud.
Bandwidth. B = (Rs/2)(1 + α) = 8000 × 1.25 = 10 000 Hz. Binary at the same bit rate: Rs = 64 000 baud, B = 32 000 × 1.25 = 40 000 Hz, four times as much.

Levels and energy. The levels are ±d, ±3d, …, ±15d, neighbours 2d apart, with 15 thresholds at 0, ±2d, …, ±14d. Average symbol energy (unit-energy pulse): Es = (2d²/16)(1² + 3² + 5² + … + 15²) = (2d²/16)(680) = 85d², which is the general (M² − 1)d²/3 = 255d²/3.

Error events. The noise sample has variance N₀/2. An inner level (14 of 16) is in error if the noise exceeds d in either direction: 2Q(d/√(N₀/2)). An end level (2 of 16) has one boundary: Q(d/√(N₀/2)).
Bit errors. With Gray labelling a symbol error to a neighbour flips one of the 4 bits, so BER ≈ 1.05 × 10⁻⁴/4 = 2.6 × 10⁻⁵.
Trade-off. 16-PAM uses a quarter of the bandwidth but needs 23.14 − 9.59 = 13.55 dB more Eb/N₀, close to the per-bit energy factor (M² − 1)/(3 log₂M) = 21.25 (13.3 dB).
Check. For M = 2 the formula gives 2(1/2)Q(√(6Eb/3N₀)) = Q(√(2Eb/N₀)), the polar result.

bank.q: Compare a zero-forcing equalizer with an adaptive LMS equalizer: noise enhancement, residual ISI, convergence and behaviour on a time-varying channel. Use the channel h<sub>−1</sub> = 0.2, h<sub>0</sub> = 1, h<sub>1</sub> = 0.3 with three taps and white noise of variance σ² = 0.1 per sample for numbers.
outline: ZF: solve for taps; forces zero ISI at the forced instants
Noise gain Σc<sub>k</sub>² and the MSE split into ISI and noise
LMS: c(n + 1) = c(n) + μe(n)x(n); tends to the MMSE taps
MMSE taps and MSE against ZF at σ² = 0.1
Convergence, step size, tracking, training and decision-directed modes
answer: ZF taps. Forcing v−1 = 0, v0 = 1, v1 = 0 gives c = (−0.2273, 1.1364, −0.3409), leaving v−2 = −0.0455 and v2 = −0.1023. Peak distortion drops from 0.5 to 0.148.

ZF noise enhancement. Output noise = σ²Σck² = 0.1 × 1.459 = 0.1459. The channel's |H(f)| = |1 + 0.2ej2πfT + 0.3e−j2πfT| falls to 0.5 at f = 1/(2T), where ZF has gain about 2: that is where the noise is boosted.

answer.pre:
MSE = residual ISI power + output noise
    = (0.0455² + 0.1023²) + 0.1459
    = 0.0125 + 0.1459 = 0.1584

answer.text: LMS. The update ck(n + 1) = ck(n) + μe(n)x(n − k), with e(n) = d(n) − y(n), is a stochastic-gradient descent on E[e²]. Its average end point is the MMSE (Wiener) solution c = R⁻¹p, with R the correlation matrix of the tap inputs (noise included) and p their correlation with the wanted symbol. For this channel:

answer: Reading the table. At σ² = 0.1 MMSE leaves more ISI but much less noise and wins by 0.158/0.127 = 1.24 (0.95 dB). At low noise (σ² = 0.01) the two nearly agree, and the MMSE taps (−0.201, 1.095, −0.294) approach the ZF taps.

Convergence. ZF is computed once from a known channel (a matrix solve). LMS starts from (0, 1, 0) and needs many symbols; in the chapter's example two training updates with μ = 0.1 moved the taps to (−0.034, 1.034, −0.060) and the squared error from 0.25 to 0.0099. A larger μ converges faster but leaves more tap jitter (excess MSE); too large a μ diverges.

Time-varying channels. ZF must re-measure the channel and re-solve. LMS tracks a slow change automatically, first with a training sequence and then decision-directed, using â(n) − y(n) as the error. A burst of wrong decisions can mislead it, so systems retrain when the error grows.
Verdict. ZF suits a known channel at high SNR; an adaptive LMS (MMSE) equalizer suits real lines and radio paths whose response is unknown and changing, and wins whenever noise matters.

bank.q: A baseband link must carry 9600 bit/s through a channel that passes 0 to 3000 Hz, with symbol error probability at most 10⁻⁵ in AWGN. Evaluate binary, 4-PAM and 8-PAM with raised cosine pulses: which are possible, which roll-off each allows, what E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ each needs, and which you would choose and why.
outline: R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/log₂M and B = (R<sub>s</sub>/2)(1 + α) ≤ 3000 Hz
Binary impossible (needs at least 4800 Hz)
Required E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ from the M-PAM formula
Timing margin, filter difficulty, equalization; final choice
answer: Bandwidth rule. With M levels, Rs = 9600/log₂M baud and B = (Rs/2)(1 + α). The channel requires B ≤ 3000 Hz, so α ≤ 6000/Rs − 1.
Binary is out. Even with the ideal sinc it needs 4800 Hz. Duobinary would not help either: it also occupies Rs/2 = 4800 Hz.

answer.text: Power needed. From Pe = 2(1 − 1/M)Q(x) with x² = 6Es/((M² − 1)N₀) and Es = Eb log₂M:

answer: Power comparison. 8-PAM needs 18.29 − 13.75 = 4.54 dB more Eb/N₀ than 4-PAM, nearly three times the transmit power for the same noise.

answer.text: In watts. Received power P = (Eb/N₀)·N₀·Rb. Taking N₀ = 10⁻⁹ W/Hz as an example:

answer: Timing in seconds. 4-PAM has T = 1/4800 = 208.3 µs, so a 0.1T clock error is 20.8 µs; 8-PAM has T = 312.5 µs and 0.1T = 31.3 µs. The slower 8-PAM symbols tolerate more absolute jitter.

Timing and filters. 4-PAM must use α = 0.25 exactly at the band edge: a steep filter and a narrower eye. For binary data the worst-case sample 0.1T off the centre is 0.652 at α = 0.25 against 0.785 at α = 0.5; for 4-PAM, whose eyes are a third as tall, the same timing error eats a larger share of each small eye. 8-PAM at α = 0.5 has 600 Hz of spare band and gentler filters, but seven thresholds and eyes a seventh as tall.
Equalization. Either scheme needs an equalizer if the real channel is not flat; 4-PAM working at the band edge is more sensitive to channel roll-off near 3000 Hz.
Eye check. In both cases the eye pattern at the receive-filter output should be watched: the vertical opening must keep the 10⁻⁵ margin, and the horizontal opening must cover the clock jitter.

Choice. 4-PAM with α = 0.25 and an adaptive equalizer: it meets the bandwidth exactly and needs about 4.5 dB less power than 8-PAM. Choose 8-PAM only if the channel edge near 3000 Hz is poor or the clock jitter is large, and the extra power is available.
Check. 4-PAM: (4800/2)(1.25) = 3000 Hz ≤ 3000 Hz. 8-PAM: (3200/2)(1.5) = 2400 Hz. Both meet the channel; binary's 4800 Hz does not.

bank.q: Explain why the matched filter is optimum in AWGN. Then evaluate the loss when (a) a rectangular pulse's matched filter is sampled at 0.9T, (b) a ramp pulse s(t) = At/T is received with an integrate-and-dump filter. Find what each loss does to a polar link designed for P<sub>e</sub> = 10⁻⁵ (E<sub>b</sub>/N₀ = 9.59 dB).
outline: Cauchy-Schwarz: SNR ≤ 2E/N₀, equality only for h = s(T − t) at t = T
Mismatch factor ρ² = ⟨h<sub>r</sub>, s⟩²/(‖h<sub>r</sub>‖²‖s‖²)
(a) triangle output 0.9E: loss 0.92 dB
(b) ramp with flat filter: ρ² = 3/4, loss 1.25 dB
New P<sub>e</sub> from Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N₀)) with the loss
answer: Why optimum. For any filter, the output SNR at t = T is [∫h(τ)s(T − τ)dτ]²/((N₀/2)∫h²dτ). Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the numerator by ∫h²dτ · E, so SNR ≤ 2E/N₀, with equality only when h(τ) ∝ s(T − τ). No linear filter can do better, and the bound is reached only at t = T.

answer.text: Mismatch in general. Write hr(t) = h(T − t), the filter's reference shape. Then

answer: ρ is the correlation coefficient between the reference and the pulse; the loss in dB is 10 log₁₀ρ².

(a) Late sample. For a rectangle of height A, the matched-filter output is the triangle y(t) = A²t for 0 ≤ t ≤ T, so y(0.9T) = 0.9E. The noise variance is still (N₀/2)E, because the noise is stationary. SNR = (0.9E)²/((N₀/2)E) = 0.81 × 2E/N₀: a loss of 10 log₁₀ 0.81 = −0.92 dB.

answer.pre:
E = ∫₀ᵀ (At/T)² dt = A²T/3
flat filter output at T: ∫₀ᵀ (At/T) dt = AT/2,   noise (N₀/2)T
SNR = (AT/2)² / ((N₀/2)T) = A²T/(2N₀)
matched: 2E/N₀ = 2A²T/(3N₀)
ratio = (1/2)/(2/3) = 3/4

answer: So ρ² = 0.75, a loss of −1.25 dB.

answer.text: Effect on the polar link. The design point Eb/N₀ = 9.59 dB gives Pe = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. Subtracting each loss and evaluating Q(√(2Eb/N₀)):

answer: Evaluation. Losses of only 1 to 2 dB multiply the error rate by 6 to 32, because Q(x) falls so steeply. The design must either keep the clock within a few per cent of T or carry a margin of 1 to 2 dB.

In a real data stream. A timing error also moves every neighbour off its zero crossing, adding ISI (see ISI and the Nyquist criterion), so the real loss is larger than this single-pulse figure; the eye pattern's horizontal opening shows how much timing error the link can take.
Remedies. A timing-recovery loop (early-late gate) keeps the sample near T; a receive filter matched to the actual pulse shape removes the mismatch loss.
Check. 10 log₁₀ 0.81 = −0.915 and 10 log₁₀ 0.75 = −1.249, so the effective values 9.59 − 0.92 = 8.67 dB and 9.59 − 1.25 = 8.34 dB used in the table are consistent.

glossary.def: The part of a symbol's sample that comes from the tails of other symbols' pulses.
D = Σ<sub>n≠0</sub>|p(nT)|/p(0), the worst-case ISI as a fraction of the wanted sample.
R<sub>s</sub>/2 = 1/(2T) hertz, the least bandwidth in which zero-ISI signalling is possible.
One symbol per second, the unit of symbol rate R<sub>s</sub> = 1/T.
Any pulse that is zero at every sampling instant except its own, so it causes no ISI.
sin(πt/T)/(πt/T): the Nyquist pulse of least bandwidth, non-causal and with slowly decaying 1/t tails.
α, 0 ≤ α ≤ 1: the excess bandwidth of a raised cosine as a fraction of R<sub>s</sub>/2.
A filter with |G(f)| = √P(f); one at each end of the link gives a raised cosine overall and a matched receiver.
Received traces overlaid in step with the symbol clock; the opening shows noise and timing margins.
A receiver filter, usually a tapped delay line, that cancels ISI caused by the channel.
An equalizer whose taps force the combined response to 1 at the centre and 0 at chosen neighbouring instants.
The rise in output noise when an equalizer has large gain where the channel is weak; Σc<sub>k</sub>² for white noise.
The update c<sub>k</sub>(n + 1) = c<sub>k</sub>(n) + μe(n)x(n − k), with e(n) the desired symbol minus the equalizer output.
An equalizer that minimises the mean-square error from ISI and noise together.
A view in which each signal is a point whose coordinates are its inner products with orthonormal basis functions.
Unit-energy, mutually orthogonal functions used as the axes of the signal space.
Builds an orthonormal basis from a set of signals by subtracting projections and normalising what is left.
The filter h(t) = s(T − t), which gives the largest SNR, 2E/N₀, at t = T in white noise.
A multiplier and integrate-and-dump that forms ∫₀ᵀ r(t)s(t)dt, the matched filter's sample at T.
Additive white Gaussian noise: flat power spectral density N₀/2 and Gaussian amplitudes.
Q(x), the probability that a unit Gaussian exceeds x; Q(x) = ½ erfc(x/√2).
Choosing the signal that makes the received vector most likely; in AWGN, the nearest signal point.
The set of received points decided as one signal; in AWGN bounded by perpendicular bisectors.
An upper bound on symbol error probability: the sum of the pairwise error probabilities.
Correlative coding with c<sub>k</sub> = a<sub>k</sub> + a<sub>k−1</sub>: binary data in R<sub>s</sub>/2 with three levels.
p<sub>k</sub> = b<sub>k</sub> ⊕ p<sub>k−1</sub> before a duobinary coder, so each bit is read from one sample and errors do not propagate.
Pulse amplitude modulation with M equally spaced levels, carrying log₂M bits per symbol.
Assigning bit patterns so that neighbouring levels differ in one bit.
